prize_parts.citation: For foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and staggered price and wage setting, and to the microfounded New Keynesian framework and policy rules that underpin modern monetary policy analysis.

statement.case_for: B014 passes the common criteria on originality, scope, durability and practical consequence. Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's welfare-based synthesis are three conceptually distinct building blocks. Together they are the standard framework for monetary policy analysis and have shaped how central banks think about rules, inflation targeting and policy trade-offs for roughly four decades. The ideas have been tested, extended and criticised in the literature and in policy institutions, so maturity is not in doubt. The trio is also the most common proposal among colleagues (six of nine members who ranked this candidate proposed it as submitted or with one name changed), but I treat that only as a coincidence of views, not as evidence of merit. My case rests on the three contributions being separable and each having a clear originating paper or body of work. After hearing colleagues, I keep a single-part prize rather than pairing B014 with a second achievement. The three-person cap would force a split of the macro credit, and the attribution is cleaner as one coherent discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The ballot lists eight names, and a three-person cap necessarily excludes Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose NK Phillips curve, estimation and medium-scale model work made the framework quantitatively usable. A prize that honours the theoretical originators may be read as overlooking the empirical strand that made the models operational in central banks. There is also a substantive concern about performance. The framework was challenged after 2008 and again in the 2021-23 inflation episode, and some core ingredients, such as the Phillips curve slope and the treatment of heterogeneity, are contested. Finally, earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, DSGE methods, time-series macro) cover adjacent ground, so the Committee may judge the marginal contribution of another monetary-macro prize differently.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B014 first with the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio, but flags that the crowded list makes the three-name choice sensitive. He also notes that the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Smets strand of medium-scale DSGE estimation is a close alternative, and that post-2008 and post-2021 episodes may affect how the framework's validity is seen.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the identification of the building blocks. I qualify one point. The medium-scale estimation strand is a distinct achievement from the theoretical framework: it concerns identifying monetary transmission from data and making the models quantitatively usable. Within a three-person cap it cannot be added without displacing one of the originators. I would not treat the post-2021 inflation episode as a challenge to the contribution itself. It is a test of the models' empirical performance, and a prize for the conceptual framework does not claim that every parametrisation fits every episode. I do take his point that the Committee should be explicit about which of the two strands, theory or estimation, it means to honour.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B014 third, proposing Woodford, Taylor and Gali rather than Calvo. He notes that credit is spread across many contributors and that Gertler's earlier recognition (2022) complicates his inclusion.
responses.response: I would keep Calvo over Gali. Calvo's 1983 pricing device is the specific building block used in nearly every NK model, and the framework cannot be told without it. Gali's contributions, including the NK Phillips curve and the Clarida-Gali-Gertler policy analysis, are important but sit on top of Calvo pricing and substantially overlap with Woodford's synthesis in what they demonstrate. On Gertler, I think the premise needs correcting. The 2022 prize went to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig, not Gertler, so Gertler's absence from my trio rests on attribution and on how much of his work is the financial-accelerator strand, not on prior recognition. I accept that Gali and Gertler have strong claims and that the cut is contestable.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 sixth and proposes Woodford, Gali and Gertler as the most synthetic contributors. He stresses the severe credit-allocation problem across at least eight names, mixed empirical evidence on the Phillips curve, and that prior macro prizes already cover nearby ground.
responses.response: I share the diagnosis of the attribution problem, but I draw a different conclusion about who to credit. A trio of Woodford, Gali and Gertler leaves out the originators of the two ingredients that define the framework, staggered pricing (Calvo) and the policy rule with staggered contracts (Taylor). It credits the synthesis and application layer without them. I find the argument about prior macro prizes the more serious one. Rational-expectations and DSGE methodology were recognised for methodological advances, whereas this achievement is about the nominal-rigidity mechanism and the policy framework, which was not itself the subject of those awards. I agree that the mixed evidence on the Phillips curve is a real caveat. It argues for careful citation wording, not for dismissing the contribution.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B016 first, proposing Persson and Tabellini, and ranks B042 second and B014 third, with the same Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio. He sees political economics as established without being redundant after the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: I agree with his trio for B014 and with his assessment that its maturity is not a concern. On B016, I recognise the case: a coherent field, decades of development, and a clear core group. I placed it outside my top eight mainly because of the partial thematic overlap with the 2024 prize and the contested cross-country identification that several colleagues, including Hassler himself, flag. I would want that identification issue resolved before ranking it above the macro candidates. That is a comparative judgement under common criteria, not a view that the field lacks merit. I note that Hassler is a long-standing co-author of mine and that this is a disclosed connection, not an adjudicated one.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would prefer to honour the theoretical originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or the estimation and empirical-synthesis strand (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gali, Gertler, Smets). The three-person cap makes these difficult to combine.

How much weight the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experience should carry in assessing the framework, given that evidence on the Phillips curve slope and on the role of heterogeneity remains mixed.

Whether support for B014 is robust once colleagues compare the trio against B010 and B042, where attribution is cleaner (two names each) but overlap with other trade or 2022-prize themes must be weighed.
I have not independently verified citation counts or priority claims. The attribution judgements rest on my own reading of the literature and on colleagues' stated views.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the proposed laureates (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is apparent from the supplied profile; none appears among my documented co-authors. I disclose that I co-author with Timo Boppart (co-opted member) and John Hassler (chair), both of whom ranked B014 highly, and that my own heterogeneous-agent work is adjacent to non-shortlisted candidates, so I do not rely on it here. These are disclosures, not adjudicated conflicts.
